name: Julian Reyes

biography.name: Julian Reyes

background.family: Lives with parents and a younger sister; family members respect separate downtime and also enjoy lively shared meals.
background.finances: Stable working-class income; family can support local education more easily than residential options.
background.geography: Corpus Christi, Texas, near coastal parks and a public library.
background.cultureLanguages: Filipino American household using English and some Tagalog; relatives communicate through frequent family calls.
background.school: Public high school; fictional autism diagnosed at seven, with written expectations, sensory breaks, and explicit group-work roles.
background.accessOpportunities: Has library clubs and coastal volunteers available; he chooses settings that explain routines clearly rather than avoiding all groups.

timeline.story: Julian liked reenacting favorite picture books with his father and insisted that the dragon receive a different voice from the narrator. He could enjoy visitors but often needed a quiet room after busy family gatherings.

An autism evaluation helped adults understand his sensory needs and difficulty with indirect instructions. Written routines reduced arguments, and a teacher learned that inviting him into a game worked better than waiting for him to infer an opening.

He became interested in tide pools and used drawings to compare animals seen on different visits. He also developed a friendship through telling deliberately terrible jokes, challenging adults who assumed factual interests described his entire social life.

During remote school he liked predictable lessons but missed library afternoons with his friend. They began writing a ridiculous adventure story by exchanging chapters, and Julian learned to leave plot decisions unresolved for the other writer.

He tried a coastal cleanup group with clear meeting instructions and specific tasks. The first crowded briefing was difficult; a volunteer later provided a written version, allowing him to participate without having to endure the same barrier each time.

In a group history project he asked for explicit responsibilities rather than doing all the research alone. He enjoyed interviewing his grandmother, but found ambiguous peer feedback harder than the actual writing and requested more specific comments.

Julian now writes fiction with his friend, volunteers occasionally, and takes challenging history courses. He is exploring college and training environments for both access and intellectual interest; support needs vary by setting, and he wants choices based on lived experience rather than predictions.
